summary.value: Small water-soaked lesions develop a white center then enlarge with concentric zones, turning brown to purplish with red or purple margins surrounded by yellowish tissue; in moist weather the spot surface becomes covered with a brownish black, powdery fungal growth, and in severe cases lesions coalesce to blight the entire leaf, which then wilts and dies.

In moist weather, the spot's surface usually becomes covered with a brownish black, powdery fungus growth.

value: Rotate crops / practice long (three-year or longer) rotations with unrelated, non-host crops such as small grains and corn.
Avoid excessive nitrogen applications; apply adequate but not excessive nitrogen fertilizer before bulb initiation.
Bury or dispose of culls and other plant debris; destroy old onion cull piles, debris, and volunteers.
Use pathogen-free, high quality seed and transplants.
Reduce hours of leaf wetness by plant spacing and density, as well as irrigation management.
Avoid dense plantings of late maturing varieties.
Avoid injuring onions during production.
Undercut roots and harvest at full maturity in dry weather; properly cure bulbs in the field, lifting and drying several days before topping with ambient to warm (90 to 95Â°F) air.
Maintain storage temperatures near 32Â°F with 70% or less relative humidity.
Plant tolerant or resistant varieties. 'Fiesta' is tolerant.
Use fungicides as soon as the disease is confirmed/occurs to prevent further spread.

treatments.quote: Cultural control Use pathogen-free seed. Practice long rotations with unrelated crops. Reduce hours of leaf wetness by plant spacing and density, as well as irrigation management. Destroy old onion cull piles and bury field debris. Avoid injuring onions during production. Properly cure bulbs in the field; lift and allow them to dry several days before topping. Plant tolerant or resistant varieties. 'Fiesta' is tolerant.

conflicts.note: PNW Handbook lists Macrosporium porri as a synonym of Alternaria porri ('Alternaria porri (syn. = Macrosporium porri)'). No taxonomy validation was supplied to confirm the currently accepted name.

affected_parts.quote: Slightly pale spots develop first on leaves or seed stalks, later taking on a light brown or purplish shade.

summary.value: At the field level, symptoms appear as circular clumps of yellowed plants a few to many feet in diameter; on individual plants leaf tissue becomes pale green, then tan to brown or yellow, and finally collapses, with lesions sometimes showing a violet-to-purple color. When leaves are wet or humidity is very high, fine, furry, grayish-white growths appear on the surface of older leaves, and systemically infected plants may be dwarfed, distorted, and pale green.
summary.quote: At the field level, symptoms of downy mildew are first noticed as circular clumps of yellowed plants that are a few to many feet in diameter. ... On individual plants, leaf tissue becomes pale green, then tan to brown or yellow, and finally collapses. Lesions may exhibit a violet-to-purple color. When leaves are wet, or when humidity is very high, signs of Peronospora destructor are visible on the surface of older leaves as fine, furry, grayish-white growths .

value: Plant only pathogen-free transplants, sets, and seed (use disease-free bulbs, sets, and seed).
Practice a 3-year or longer crop rotation away from Allium crops in fields where the disease has occurred.
Avoid poorly drained soils and select fields that are well drained.
Plant in fields with good air movement and align rows with the prevailing winds; manage plant density/spacing and limit intercropping to reduce humidity.
Avoid overhead/sprinkler irrigation; use drip or sub-surface irrigation, or adjust irrigation to maximize leaf drying.
Change planting date to avoid a full canopy during conditions favorable for downy mildew.
Destroy onion plant refuse, cull piles, residue, volunteer plants, and eradicate wild Allium spp.
Avoid over-application of nitrogen, which promotes succulent leaves and disease.
Avoid entering fields when leaves are wet and avoid injuring the crop with herbicides and other materials.
Use resistant red onion cultivars (e.g., Calred) where available (resistance active in flower stalks, not leaves).
Spray at the first sign of disease and rotate fungicides among different mode-of-action groups; ensure thorough foliar coverage.
Use the DOWNCAST forecast program to optimize field scouting and spray timing.

Seed treatment with a metalaxyl/mefenoxam formulation; foliar fungicides including Actigard (P1), copper (M1), CAA-fungicides/Revus/Forum (40), chlorothalonil (M5: Bravo, Echo 720), mancozeb (M3), Ridomil Gold MZ/Bravo (mefenoxam mixes), Omega 500F/fluazinam (29), phosphonates (P7), Presidio (43), Regalia (P5), Milstop, strobilurins (11), Zampro (ametoctradin/dimethomorph), Orondis Ultra (oxathiapiprolin/mandipropamid), Reason 500 SC (fenamidone).
Biological control: Actinovate AG, Double Nickel LC, Sonata, Stargus.
treatments.quote: To reduce the incidence and severity of downy mildew: Minimize canopy leaf wetness: Avoid sprinkler irrigation, especially when the canopy begins to fill. ... Spray at the first sign of the disease. After the first spray, scout fields and make subsequent applications when weather conditions are favorable for the disease. Rotate with fungicides from different mode-of-action groups to reduce the risk of fungicide resistance development.

conflicts.note: Both sources agree on leaves and seed/flower stalks; UC IPM additionally notes the pathogen can infect bulbs systemically (whole plant), while PNW explicitly lists seed stalks.
Only PNW characterizes the pathogen type, describing P. destructor as a 'fungus-like microorganism' (i.e., an oomycete); UC IPM does not state a disease type.
